title: The true bargain
hookLine: sent with twenty rupees to strike a good deal, he feeds hungry holy men and comes home empty-handed
last: THE COBRA'S SHADE — SOMETHING SHELTERS YOU.

lines: NOT THE DEAL HIS FATHER MEANT.
cards: Mehta Kalu has had enough. His son is a young man now, and he still hasn't shown the slightest interest in making money. The buffaloes wandered.

The lessons turned into questions. So the father tries one more thing, the thing a practical man would try. He counts out twenty rupees, a real sum, puts it in his son's hand, and says: go to the market town.
Buy something you can sell for more. Make a good deal. Bring back a profit.
The son nods, takes the money, and sets off down the road. He does make a deal. Just not the one his father meant.

teach.h: HOLY MEN WHO HADN'T EATEN IN DAYS.
teach.b: On the way, the story says, Nanak came across a group of holy men sitting by the road. Wandering ascetics, thin, quiet. He stopped and talked with them and found out they hadn't eaten in days.
He looked at the twenty rupees.
He thought about his father's words: make a good deal, a true one. And he went into the town and spent every coin on flour, lentils, butter and other food, brought it back and fed them all.
Then he walked home with empty hands. Sacha sauda. Sacha means true.
Sauda means a deal, a trade, a bargain. The true bargain. Nanak's answer to his father's instruction was that feeding the hungry was the truest deal there was.
You didn't lose twenty rupees; you traded them for something that doesn't run out.
His father didn't see it that way. The janamsakhis say Mehta Kalu was furious, and some tellings say he struck his son. Others in the family, and Rai Bular, stepped in to calm him.
It's an honest touch in the story: the Guru's family didn't always understand him, and it hurt.

teach.h: AN EARLY SEED OF THE LANGAR.
teach.b: Sikhs often see in this moment an early seed of the langar you met on day two: food for anyone hungry, bought with honest money, given freely.

And there's a gurdwara today called Sacha Sauda, in Pakistan, on the spot where tradition says the holy men were fed. Nanak didn't disobey his father's words. He obeyed them more deeply than his father intended.
Make a true deal, the father said. So he did.

how: Sikhs tell the story of sacha sauda as an early sign of the langar and of Guru Nanak's teaching on sharing; Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Pakistan marks the place tradition connects with it.

o: a wandering holy man's vow to own nothing at all
the true bargain: money spent feeding the hungry
the money a son owes his father's business

games.q: you've been given twenty rupees to make a good deal. on the road you meet holy men who haven't eaten in days. what do you do?
o: keep walking. the money is for business.
spend it all on food and feed them.
give them a rupee and go on.
games.why: Nanak spent every coin on food, fed them, and called it the true bargain: sacha sauda.

practice: Settle, and think without guilt about where your money went this week: coffee, rent, something online.
Now imagine holding twenty dollars, just as Nanak held twenty rupees, and picture someone who's hungry: a stranger on your street, a neighbor who's struggling, a food bank shelf.
Picture that twenty turning into a meal in their hands, and sit with how that deal feels.

wordCard.voice: Sacha sauda. The true bargain: twenty rupees traded for a meal for the hungry, the best deal Nanak could make.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: sacha (true) + sauda (a deal, a bargain).

carryVoice: Your line: the best bargain. He walked home with empty hands. Until tomorrow.
